newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Land sales ban reflects Israel, PLO peace crisis.
newsitem.headline: Land sales ban reflects Israel, PLO peace crisis.

text.p: Reflecting the near-total paralysis in Israel-PLO peace moves, a Palestinian ban on land sales to Jews and a pair of West Bank killings have overshadowed talk of a resumption of frozen talks.
Israel has linked a Palestinian Authority decision to ban the selling of land to Israelis with the recent killings of two Palestinian land dealers accused of doing just that.
Farid Bashiti, 70, and Harbi Abu Sarah, in his sixties, were found dead in PLO-ruled Ramallah within 10 days of each other.
The killings followed remarks by Palestinian Justice Minister Freih Abu Medein that a Jordanian law setting the death penalty for those who sold land to Israelis remained in force in the West Bank.
The Palestinian Authority has denied any involvement in the killings, now being separately investigated by Israel and the Palestinians, but has defended its ban on land sales.

The controversy is a reflection of how the deeply suspicious sides view the present peace crisis, triggered by Israel's groundbreaking on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March and deepened by a Moslem militant's bombing of a Tel Aviv cafe three days later.
Netanyahu on Monday seized on the ban -- and the killings -- to bolster his charge that the present deadlock stems from PLO use of violence and "terror" as a means of pressure in peace talks.
"I think it's ghastly, just monstrous, to issue a law that says that anyone who sells land to Jews will be executed," Netanyahu told reporters in parliament.
Nabil Abu Rdaineh, an aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, said on Monday the ban was necessary to combat the spread of Jewish settlements in occupied lands they want for a future state.

"The Palestinian law is not a racist law. It was issued to protect Palestinians and their land from attempts to steal and seize Palestinian land in illegal ways, especially Arab Jerusalem," Abu Rdaineh told Reuters.

Palestinians say Israelis have been buying land in the West Bank, including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, to block a political agreement which they hope will end Israeli rule in the areas captured by the Jewish state in the 1967 Middle East war.
The tumult surrounding the land ban captures in a nutshell one U.S. official's assessment of the breakdown of trust that threatens the 1993 Israeli-PLO interim Oslo peace accords.
"The core bargain of Oslo has broken down," U.S. ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk told the Israel-U.S. Chamber of Commerce on Sunday.
"Terrorism on the one side and unilateral acts which have created the impression that the final status issues are being pre-empted on the other have combined to break this trust," Indyk said.

The broad-brush Oslo accords promising security for Israel and self-rule for Palestinians were aimed at building mutual confidence before they tackled thorny "final status" issues including the fate of Jerusalem and Jewish settlements.

Netanyahu told parliament on Monday Israel would not return to its pre-1967 borders and that Palestinians suffered from a "crisis of expectations" about their goal to found an independent state in yet-to-resume final status talks.

"Chairman Arafat has no trust in the government of Israel and it will take a lot of time and many steps until the situation can gradually stabilise," Arafat's aide Ahmed Tibi told Israel's Army radio.
"I don't know if it's possible," Tibi said.
